h: Do not be late this time, My Lords: justice delayed is justice denied
dek: S. Raghotham argues that if the Supreme Court puts off its ruling this time too, as it did with electoral bonds and Bihar's SIR, the court's door will mean nothing to the 13.3 crore people struck off the rolls and the protesters being beaten on the streets.
body: Bengaluru-based senior journalist S. Raghotham has made a direct appeal to the judges of the Supreme Court: do not be late this time. The electoral bonds case dragged on for nearly six years and two general elections, and in that time the BJP received Rs 8,200 crore. Petitions on Bihar's SIR were filed in July 2025, but the verdict came on 27 May 2026, after the state had already voted, even though the question concerned seven crore voters.

The writer recalls Delhi on 10 October: the city sealed, 45 metro stations shut, more than 250 trains cancelled and about 25,000 police and paramilitary personnel deployed. Thousands of people were detained, among them lawyers, journalists and leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party. There have also been allegations of sexual harassment and assault.

The writer also questions the court's own role. On 9 October it suggested other sites for the sit-in, and after that the police withdrew Jantar Mantar's status altogether. On 11 October a Sunday bench said peaceful protesters cannot be detained unlawfully. Then 46 petitions were tagged together, but on a complaint from Connaught Place traders the court also promised to balance the two sides.

At the root is a 2023 law that removed the Chief Justice from the panel that picks election commissioners and seated a cabinet minister in his place. The court refused to stay it in March 2024, Gyanesh Kumar took office in February 2025, and on 23 September two judges split on whether to send the matter to a Constitution bench. Meanwhile, according to the writer, 13.3 crore names have been cut from the rolls.

Raghotham has three demands: that the right to protest be recognised without ifs and buts, that the petitions on police excesses be heard at once, and that the 2023 law be decided within weeks. Otherwise citizens will conclude that they have nothing to get from the court.
nazar: This article is not an attack on the court but a plea to its last hope. When the government holds a majority in Parliament and the Election Commission dodges questions, the burden of protecting the Constitution falls on the court. If the verdict comes after the election, then for those whose names were cut, that is the poor, migrant workers, Muslims, Dalits and women, it remains only a footnote in history.
Weighing the right to protest on a scale of balance is a dangerous road. The traders' inconvenience is real, but it cannot equal the voice of citizens.
sawal: Whom does justice serve if it comes after the election?
ref: Election Commissioners Act 2023

The law on appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and commissioners, which replaced the Chief Justice on the selection committee with a Union minister chosen by the Prime Minister. This gives the government a majority on the committee.
Electoral bonds
A scheme for anonymous donations to political parties. The Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional in 2024, but by then several elections had already been fought with its help.
ank: personnel deployed in Delhi on 10 October

h: Peace bond: conditions on dissent in the name of peace
dek: Constitutional lawyer Shubham Kumar explains which colonial law the peace bond demanded from Neha Bora comes from, and why, without any conviction, it can become a tool to keep students off the streets.
body: A Special Executive Magistrate has demanded a peace bond of Rs 10,000 and a surety from AISA president Neha Bora. Constitutional lawyer Shubham Kumar asks whether this is an effort to keep the peace or a curb on dissent. Protesters who stay home out of fear are no proof of peace.

Bora was detained on 16 October on her way to Mandi House. According to the police, 40-50 people moved towards Barakhamba Road shouting slogans. The next day a notice came, listing prohibited protest and sloganeering. Bora has not been convicted of any crime; the police only have a suspicion. On 23 October the Delhi High Court did not quash the notice, but said Bora must be given all the material the notice rests on.

The writer explains that the peace bond is a power from British rule that survived even in the new Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (criminal procedure code). Under Section 126, proceedings can begin without an FIR and without a conviction, and a bond of up to one year can be demanded. These magistrates are appointed by the government, and in Delhi they are even police officers. That is why an independent check of police allegations is essential.

His main argument is that an FIR is only an allegation, taking part in past protests is no proof of violence, and breaking a prohibitory order is not by itself a reason for a bond. If the ban under Section 163 and the bond under Section 126 run together, the breach of one order will itself become proof of a future threat. From the Madhu Limaye case (1970) to Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the court has placed strict conditions on such powers.

The writer reminds us that even without a conviction, repeated court dates, lawyers' fees, the hunt for a surety and the fear of detention can silence students. Under Article 19 the state's job is to make arrangements for peaceful assembly, not to treat dissent as disorder.
nazar: The real target of the peace bond is the student who has neither money for a lawyer nor a surety. Neha Bora's refusal matters because it puts this quiet punishment in front of everyone.

In a country where those who shout hate slogans roam free without notices, and those who speak of the Constitution are asked for bonds, peace comes to mean nothing more than the convenience of those in power.
sawal: Whose peace is it when speaking is not allowed?
ref: Peace bond (Section 126)
A magistrate can take a written promise and surety from a person that they will not break the peace for a set period. No conviction for any crime is needed for this.
Madhu Limaye vs SDM, Monghyr (1970)
A seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court upheld preventive provisions, but said the procedural safeguards in them must be strictly followed.

h: Patchwork will not do: bring back the pre-SIR rolls
dek: Three former senior officials argue that the Election Commission's latest fixes are temporary patches and that cutting the names of people away from home for a while is against the law, so trust will return only if the whole SIR is scrapped.
by: N.K. Sharma, Sanjay Kumar and Siraj Hussain
body: N.K. Sharma and Sanjay Kumar, two former officials of the statistics ministry, and former Union agriculture secretary Siraj Hussain say the fixes the Election Commission is making are just temporary patches. If faith in elections is to return, the whole SIR must be scrapped and the rolls restored to the state they were in before this drive.

They list a long catalogue of flaws: names cut in the name of logical discrepancies, missing voters, duplicate registrations, misuse of Form 7 and allegations of tampering with ECINet. But according to the writers, the most serious issue has been discussed the least: cutting names by marking people absent or shifted elsewhere.

Under Section 20(1A) of the Representation of the People Act 1950 and the 2023 electoral roll rules, being away for a while does not end ordinary residence if the person intends and is able to return. If a government employee from Lucknow is transferred to Delhi, his name should not be cut from Lucknow. If the place where one lives right now is treated as one's residence, then students, women who move home after marriage, nomadic communities, slum dwellers and migrant workers will be the first to be left out.

According to the writers, the Commission has itself accepted this. An advertisement on 5 August 2026 asked absent voters to fill Form 6, and an instruction on 15 October removed the declaration about relatives from Form 6. But since 2022 Form 6 is only for first-time voters, so without settling the question of residence, the promise that no voter will be left behind will not be kept.

Their suggestions: restore the old rolls; if SIR is held anywhere in future, set its method with the consent of all parties, like the model code of conduct; and do the work over about a year, not in a hurry. Until then the Centre should ask the states to restore government scheme benefits to those whose names were cut.
nazar: This article argues from the rulebook, not from slogans, and that is why it works. Taking the vote from people who drift from city to city for a living is a double punishment: first the village gave them no work, then the roll took away their identity.

If schemes like rations and pensions also go along with the name, this becomes a question not just of elections but of life. Instead of hiding its mistake in small fixes, the Commission should admit it openly.
sawal: Must someone who leaves home for a living leave their vote behind too?
ref: Ordinary residence
Under Section 20 of the Representation of the People Act 1950, the place where a person usually lives. It does not end because of a temporary absence.
Form 6 and Form 8
Form 6 is for adding a new name. After the 2022 change, Form 8 is filled for a change of address and corrections.

h: The vote chori slogan is not enough; raise the bread-and-butter question too
dek: Aditya Menon's uncomfortable warning is that the vote chori (vote theft) campaign is no magic wand for the opposition, and that too much stress on rigging just before an election can break the spirit of its own voters.
body: The Quint's political editor Aditya Menon has written something uncomfortable in his newsletter: the vote chori campaign is no magic weapon in the opposition's hands against the BJP. This is a warning not from inside the movement but from an informed observer standing outside it, yet it needs to be heard.

The first argument is about the ground. Early 2027 brings elections in UP, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Manipur and Goa, and according to the writer's ground sources, vote chori, SIR or Gyanesh Kumar has not become a major election issue in any of them. In the August 2026 Mood of the Nation survey, about half of the people agreed that democracy is in danger, yet it was not among the top five issues. Jobs, prices and economic growth were at the top.

The second argument is about boycott. According to the writer, a boycott works only when it rises from among the people. He cites Punjab in 1992, when a boycott by most Akali Dal factions brought turnout down to 25 percent, and Kashmir in the 1990s. Today a boycott called by the Congress or the Cockroach Janata Party does not look like a serious option to him.

The third argument is the most delicate: too much stress on rigging just before an election can keep one's own supporters at home. If someone is convinced the result is already fixed, why would they go to vote? So the writer says parties must strike a balance between vigilance and morale.

Menon reckons that removing Gyanesh Kumar will not be easy either, because within the BJP's circles he is seen as the man cleaning illegal migrants out of Bengal's rolls. The next round of elections will likely be held under his watch, so his advice is that the opposition return to livelihood issues as soon as it can.
nazar: Menon has a point, but also a blind spot. Vote chori and the bread question are not separate: the worker whose name was cut from the roll lost his ration and his voice along with it. The opposition's challenge is to join the two into one story, not to drop either.
Still, this warning is useful for the movement. The anger on the street will last only if it connects with the daily hardships of the village and the small town.
sawal: Is the fight for the vote separate from the fight for a livelihood?
ref: Mood of the Nation
A regular opinion survey by the India Today group that measures the country's mood, the government's popularity and the big issues on people's minds.
Punjab election 1992
An Assembly election held during the years of militancy, boycotted by most Akali factions. The Congress formed the government amid very low turnout.

h: Now the voter must prove she is a voter
dek: Dilip Khan argues that SIR has turned the legal basis of the voter roll upside down: earlier the person seeking to remove a name had to give proof, now citizens have to prove their own right.
body: Dilip Khan begins with the Supreme Court hearing of a petition against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The court said clearly that it had not approved any altered version of Form 6, though the Commission had claimed exactly this in its press note. The writer calls this a half-truth. The July 2026 declaration form, which asks a new voter whether their parents were listed in the previous SIR, never even came before the court.

The writer reminds us that since 1993 the Election Commission has been a three-member body, and the chief commissioner is first among equals, not the boss. According to the petition, commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded written objections at least 14 times in ten months.

The article's real stress is on the burden of proof. In a normal revision the existing roll is the base, and whoever objects to a name must give proof; after the 1995 Lal Babu Hussein ruling, no name can be cut on suspicion without notice and a hearing. According to the writer, SIR started the roll from zero. Whoever did not fill the enumeration form was not formally removed, just left out, so the hearing rule never applied.

In Bihar about 65 lakh names were left out of the draft, in Bengal 58 lakh, and in the 12 states of the second phase 5.18 crore. There is the example of a seat in Bengal where the losing margin was 862 votes and 5,432 names were held back in the name of verification. The writer says a vote is not a savings account; a missed vote does not come back next time.

Removing infiltrators was SIR's declared aim, but according to the writer the Commission has still not said how many foreigners were found. In one analysis from Bihar, of a hundred cases examined, seventy people turned out not to be foreigners at all.
nazar: Far from slogans, this article uses sections of law and court records to show where the movement's anger comes from. When citizens have to prove their own right again and again, the foundation of democracy cracks.
The heaviest price is being paid by migrant workers, women who move home after marriage and the landless poor, who have the fewest papers. The fight at Jantar Mantar is really their fight.
sawal: How many times must a citizen prove their vote?
ref: Lal Babu Hussein ruling (1995)
A Supreme Court ruling that no one's name can be removed from the voter roll on mere suspicion, without notice and a hearing.
Form 6
The form for adding a new name to the voter roll, laid down in the Registration of Electors Rules 1960, which only the Central government has the power to change.

h: The police that could not save our daughters are now wielding lathis
dek: An editorial in Siasat asks why the government chose nothing but force against a peaceful movement against Gyanesh Kumar.
body: This editorial in Hyderabad's Urdu daily Siasat is about the days in Delhi when the movement against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was at its peak. The paper says the government chose only force, instead of talks or restraint. People were picked up from their homes, stopped on the roads, denied transport, beaten and taken to police stations.

According to the editorial, even the Supreme Court's direction was ignored. The court had said metro stations should not be shut, yet 45 stations stayed closed and even those that were open had restrictions. Trains coming to Delhi were stopped and students and young people were detained at the stations themselves. Those heading to stations or the airport to travel to other cities showed their tickets, but no one listened.

The paper alleges that no one was spared: lawyers, journalists, the elderly, women, girls. The use of force on girls seemed like a planned scheme, detention rules were broken and often no women police were present. The CCTV cameras put up across the city also seem like an attempt to intimidate.

The editorial's sharpest point is this comparison: the same police cannot stop rapes on college campuses, attacks on girls in parks and the killing of women on the streets, and then make the excuse of broken cameras. But when students, lawyers and citizens gather peacefully for the right to vote, lathis (batons) come down at the government's signal.

In the end the paper warns the Centre and the Delhi Police that educated, aware young people cannot be brought under control the way marginalised groups were, and that this movement will not be crushed by force.
nazar: This Urdu newspaper's voice records the unease felt in the movement's first week in every home whose child had gone to Jantar Mantar. Questioning police harshness is not taking the movement's side; it is taking the Constitution's side.
When a state's police look helpless before criminals and brave before protesters, its priorities speak for themselves.
sawal: Whom are the police there to protect, the citizen or those in power?
ref: Siasat
An Urdu daily published from Hyderabad since 1949, counted among the most widely read Urdu newspapers in South India.
Jantar Mantar
A site near Parliament in New Delhi that has for decades been set aside for sit-ins and protests, and where this movement has been centred since 10 October 2026.

h: Not a clean-up of voter rolls but a takeover by software
dek: Srinivas Kodali says that behind SIR is a centralised digital machine that has algorithms, instead of booth officers, decide who stays a voter.
body: The government and the Election Commission describe SIR as a routine clean-up of the voter roll. According to Hyderabad-based independent researcher Srinivas Kodali, it is a far bigger change. The aim now is not just to remove duplicate names but to build a centralised map of every voter and their relationships, family and even marriage, and the Commission has said almost nothing about its algorithms or software.

The writer draws attention to ECINet and ERONet 2.0. TCS, the company that built it, described it in its annual report as a single source of truth for the Commission. Under the law, the final power to add or remove names lies with the Electoral Registration Officer, and the process must be transparent and include a hearing. The writer asks whether these rules have even been written into the software. If officers have been sidelined, then the machine decides and names are cut by algorithm.

Kodali sees this as a link in the same model as Aadhaar, CoWIN and Vahan, in which one central database decides everything. He recalls that in 2015 the Supreme Court halted the programme to link voter rolls with Aadhaar, but before that the same experiment in Telangana had already taken away the vote of lakhs of people. In the 2018 Assembly election there, a large number of people could not vote.

The writer does not let any one party off. According to him, the Congress pushed Aadhaar forward without a law, the Telangana experiments happened in the BRS years, and the BJP took it further. Many opposition leaders, too, kept demanding full linking with Aadhaar to fix the rolls.

Repeating Stafford Beer's maxim, he says the purpose of a system is what it does. The complaints of those left out reached officials and nothing changed, so these are not mistakes but design. He demands that limits on the use of data be written into law.
nazar: The movement hinges on Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, but Kodali reminds us that one man leaving will not stop the machine that cuts names without accountability. An open audit of the software should be a major demand of this fight.
This article is also a mirror for the opposition: many of the parties against SIR today argued yesterday for linking everything to Aadhaar.
sawal: When a machine cuts names, who will answer for it?
ref: ECINet
The Election Commission's central digital platform, which brings together about 40 apps and services including ERONet; objections to how it is run were raised even within the Commission.
Stafford Beer
A British management thinker whose maxim is that a system should be judged not by its stated intentions but by its actual results.

h: Israel's Palestinian citizens: they will vote, but expect no change
dek: On Israel's election day, Mohammad Kadan explains that for Palestinian citizens the vote is only a shield, not a way forward.
body: Israel held a general election on 27 October. For most Israelis the contest is between Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot's opposition, but for about a fifth of the population, Israel's Palestinian citizens, the question is different. According to Palestinian writer Mohammad Kadan, even the anti-Netanyahu camp offers them no assurance of reversing policies.

Kadan recalls that the Palestinians who stayed on their land after 1948 got citizenship in 1952 and lived under military rule until 1966. Citizenship came, equality did not: discriminatory laws, underfunded basic services, land seizures and state control over education and culture. The writer alleges that the government has handed the work of violence to criminal gangs, armed with weapons stolen from army stores or smuggled in, and that amid police indifference this violence has taken hundreds of lives.

He calls it a process of recolonisation. It began in 2021 in mixed cities such as Jaffa and Lydd and sped up after October 2023. In August, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's party put forward a plan to make the Naqab and northern Israel Jewish-majority, including one million new Jewish residents and 40 new settlements. Along with this, Itamar Ben-Gvir's National Guard and the three lakh gun licences issued in his time are militarising daily life.
The writer has no faith in the parliamentary route either. Mansour Abbas's Ra'am party joined the coalition that kept Netanyahu out in 2021, but could bring no fundamental change.

Still, Kadan will vote, because another term of the far right is a direct threat. But he says the vote can only slow the pace of this project. The real answer lies in grassroots organising, popular committees and reform of the High Follow-Up Committee, because the fate of these citizens is no different from that of other Palestinians.
nazar: Kadan's argument will not feel unfamiliar to readers in India. When citizenship exists on paper and equality does not exist on the ground, an election becomes for a minority a fight for survival, not for change. Plans to change the population balance of a region and armed civilian squads are tools to frighten minorities in any democracy.

In our view, the article's most important point is that the vote and grassroots organising are not substitutes for each other. For communities that institutions fail again and again, building their own institutions is the way to hold on.
sawal: Whose democracy is it where the vote does not bring equality?
ref: Naqab (Negev)
The desert region of southern Israel, home to a large number of Bedouin Palestinians. The government does not recognise many of their villages.
High Follow-Up Committee
The largest joint representative body of Israel's Palestinian citizens, made up of parties, heads of local bodies and civil society groups.

h: Lula's win: a blow to Trumpism, but Brazil is still divided
dek: According to Adriana Carranca, Lula has stopped the far right, but half the country still stands on the other side.
body: On 25 October, 80-year-old Lula da Silva was elected President of Brazil for the fourth time. He defeated far-right senator Flavio Bolsonaro with 51.79 percent of the vote and a margin of about 44 lakh votes, even though three weeks earlier, in the first round, he had been about 22 lakh votes behind. According to Brazilian journalist Adriana Carranca, this is a blow to Trump's dream of a hemisphere of governments like his own, but it would be a mistake to see it as a victory for the left.

In the first round more than three crore thirty lakh people did not vote. That was 21.08 percent, the highest since 1998. Flavio stood in for his father Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for crimes against democracy.

Unemployment was at 5.3 percent and deforestation in the Amazon at its lowest since 1988, yet voters did not give full credit. The reasons the writer lists: a growing number of workers in informal jobs that unions do not reach, young men leaning to the right, the Workers' Party's establishment image after Dilma Rousseff's impeachment in 2016, and a police system and overcrowded prisons inherited from the dictatorship, which became recruiting grounds for criminal gangs.

After the first-round shock, Lula went back to rallies and social media. Trump gave him the biggest opening. US tariffs, imposed in retaliation for Bolsonaro's trial, hit Brazilian businesses, and Lula turned the second round into a fight for national sovereignty. In the second round non-voting fell to 19.22 percent, and the Supreme Court's two-hour extension of voting helped working-class neighbourhoods.

Still, nearly half the voters chose his rival. According to the writer, Flavio has challenged the result and his party can block Lula's agenda in Congress. In her view, the fight for Brazil's democracy has only just begun.
nazar: The lesson for India is clear: good economic numbers do not turn into votes on their own unless informal workers, the young and people in insecure neighbourhoods see themselves at the centre of politics. And when a foreign power puts pressure on behalf of one side, the question of sovereignty can also unite the people.
Brazil also showed that a small court ruling, such as extending voting hours, can raise participation in poor areas. Making it easy to vote is the real protection of democracy.
sawal: Why does half a country stay angry despite good numbers?
ref: Workers' Party (PT)
Lula's left-wing party, born of labour movements in 1980. Its leaders were the country's presidents from 2003 to 2016.
Impeachment of Dilma Rousseff
In 2016 Lula's successor as president was removed on charges of breaking budget rules. Her supporters call it a parliamentary coup.

h: Sri Lanka's new terror law: softer on detention, harsher on dissent
dek: M. C. Rasmin argues that the PSTA is better written than the old PTA, but it is not a better law.
body: Sri Lanka's NPP government promised in its 2024 manifesto to repeal the notorious anti-terror law, the PTA. Now, in its place, it has brought the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, or PSTA, against which 25 petitions are pending in the Supreme Court. Dr M. C. Rasmin says the new bill is better drafted, but it is not a better law.

Look at the PTA's 47-year record. In 2011 the government itself admitted that 893 people were held under it and only 64 were being tried. In a 2020 study, 84 percent of male prisoners spoke of torture. The targets were first Tamil youth, then Muslims after the 2019 Easter attacks, then a poet, student activists and, this year, a rapper.

The writer's biggest objection is to the definition of terrorism. It contains loose words such as compelling the government 'unduly' and 'serious economic loss', which could take in strikes, boycotts or farmers blocking roads. The President can ban an organisation with no time limit, and a seven-year sentence for withholding information could turn relatives, teachers and religious leaders into informers. Phones can be seized without a warrant.

Rasmin also accepts some real reforms: magistrates will be able to inspect places of detention without notice, police questioning will be recorded, and a confession made before the police will not count as evidence. But detention will still be decided by a defence ministry official, and someone can be held for up to two years without charge.

The writer agrees that after the Easter attacks the country needs an anti-terror law, but he cites India's UAPA, under which there were 10,552 arrests between 2014 and 2020 and only 253 convictions. His demands are that protests and strikes be kept out of the definition, that every detention be decided by a court, and that use of the PTA stop right now.
nazar: Rasmin has held up India's UAPA as a warning, and that should sting us the most. When a law contains loose words like 'economic loss' or 'pressure on the government', workers, farmers, minorities and journalists are the first to fall within its reach.
In South Asia governments change, but the laws made for those who protest survive. Parties that speak against such laws in opposition often just give them a new name once in power.
sawal: How can a law that guards against terror spare dissent?
ref: PTA
The Prevention of Terrorism Act, a 1979 Sri Lankan law under which people were held for years without trial. Human rights groups have long demanded its repeal.
NPP
National People's Power, a left-leaning alliance led by Anura Kumara Dissanayake, which won the presidential and parliamentary elections in 2024.

h: Bangladesh: without reform, a long slump and high prices are certain
dek: Fahmida Khatun says weak growth is no longer a one-year problem but a sign of a deep structural crisis.
body: According to the IMF's October report, Bangladesh's growth rate will be 3.2 per cent in 2026-27 (the April estimate was 4.3), and it could slip to 2.2 per cent the following year. Average inflation is expected to be 10.9 per cent, while the government is holding on to a growth target of 6.5 per cent. Fahmida Khatun, an economist at the Centre for Policy Dialogue, says the eight-month-old government should treat this as a serious crisis.

The pressure comes from outside and from within. Wars in West Asia and costly energy are pushing up costs, and Bangladesh depends heavily on imported fuel. At home, private investment has shrunk for the second year in a row. By June 2026, 32.78 per cent of bank loans had gone bad, so banks are unable to channel people's savings into productive business.

Ordinary people are paying the price. The World Bank estimates that 2.1 million more people were pushed into poverty in 2025-26. Inflation has cut real wages and new jobs have stalled. Women's share in the workforce fell from 42.8 per cent in 2022 to 38.4 per cent in 2024.

The government's purse is also tight. Tax collection is about 8 per cent of GDP, and rising interest payments are eating into development spending. Khatun calls for making public the audit reports of weak banks, giving them time-bound plans and tying state support to strict conditions. She wants the tax net widened and an IMF programme that protects vulnerable groups.

In her view, big projects should begin only once land, design, money and procurement are settled; power purchase agreements should be made public and 'capacity payments' reviewed; and exports should move beyond readymade garments. Otherwise the country could be stuck in a long 'stagflation', and getting out of it will mean taking on vested interests.
nazar: The most important part of this warning is the people behind the numbers: 2.1 million newly poor, and women being pushed out of work. Bangladesh's success story was built by women workers in garment factories, and their loss of work puts that whole story in question.

It is a mirror for India too. Bad loans, weak tax collection and closed-door deals with power companies are familiar here as well. And when a neighbour's economy wobbles, jobs, trade and migration across the border are all affected.
sawal: Where did women's work get lost in the growth figures?
ref: Stagflation
A state in which growth stalls and unemployment rises while inflation also stays high. It is considered the hardest situation to get out of.
Capacity payment
A fixed payment the government makes to private power companies whether or not it buys their electricity. In Bangladesh it has become a heavy burden.

h: The screen's 'angry young man' is old news; now women lead on the street
dek: Aditya Vikram Singh and Sudhanshubala Sahu argue that in this year's protests young women are not the ones to be rescued, but the leaders.
by: Aditya Vikram Singh and Sudhanshubala Sahu
body: The 'angry young man' of Salim-Javed's films, the hero of Zanjeer (1973) and Deewaar (1975), took on unjust power, but he also 'protected' the women around him. Aditya Vikram Singh and Sudhanshubala Sahu, who work in sociology, write that in that cinema the woman was there to be rescued; she was not seen as someone who would stand up for herself.

The writers say the same 'protector' mindset shows up in politics. In most big mass movements women were either absent or there only for show, and despite the country having several women leaders, they are still seen as exceptions.

In 2026 the writers see a change. In the protests against the NEET paper leak in July, against rising sexual violence in September and against electoral irregularities in October, many young women were seen at the very front. They name AISA president Neha Bora, Youth Congress's Gurmehar Kaur and Sonali Yadav, president of the AISA unit at Allahabad University, whose video singing 'Inquilab aayega' (the revolution will come) with the crowd spread widely.

The article also mentions a mocking slogan going around on Instagram that pokes fun at how far men can be trusted. To the writers, this is a way of turning anger at male rules into laughter. This generation grew up watching misogynist media, but it has higher enrolment in schools and colleges and access to feminist writing too.

The screen hero, beaten by the system, staged a spectacle of violence and wrong turns, while these women are choosing the path of politics and dissent. They are neither victims nor idols, but leaders who ask power uncomfortable questions. According to the writers, this is a cultural jolt that could make Indian politics better.
nazar: This article rests not on data but on a changing mood, and that is both its strength and its limit. To us, the real question is when this leadership seen on the street will reach parties, unions and legislatures, where tickets and decisions are handed out.

We must also remember that women in villages and in Dalit and Adivasi (indigenous) settlements have led fights over land, water, prohibition of liquor and wages for years. It is not right to forget that long tradition in the new glare of the camera.
sawal: When will leadership on the street reach a seat in Parliament?
ref: Angry young man
Amitabh Bachchan's character in films written by Salim-Javed, a lone hero angry with the system. He is seen as a symbol of the restlessness of the 1970s.

h: Iran war: two leaders' seats, a whole region at stake
dek: Majid Ali Noonari argues that the domestic politics of Netanyahu and Trump could inflame the Iran war instead of ending it.
body: The Iran war, which began on 28 February 2026, has passed eight months. Majid Ali Noonari of the University of Sindh believes the war may be in its final phase, but that the biggest danger comes from the political compulsions of two leaders: Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump.

Israel held an election on 27 October. In the surveys the writer cites, Netanyahu's coalition was getting about 50 seats and Gadi Eisenkot's coalition a majority in the 120-seat parliament. The US has midterm elections on 3 November. According to the writer, the war has pushed up fuel prices and inflation there, Trump's approval stands at 36 per cent, and he needs a deal that opens the Hormuz route and brings oil from 117 dollars a barrel to below 100.
There is a tug of war inside Israel too. There are reports that Netanyahu wanted a new strike on Iran, and army chief Eyal Zamir opposed it, warning of a misjudgement.

The writer lists several signs of rising tension: American aircraft carriers in West Asia and advice to diplomats' families to leave Gulf countries. According to him, Iran has split its Revolutionary Guard into 31 provincial commands that can fight without orders from the centre, and has threatened to target even undersea cables, desalination plants and power stations. Many of the article's claims come without named sources, so they should be read as the writer's own assessment.

Pakistan, Qatar, Turkey and Russia are talking with Tehran about enriched uranium, opening Hormuz and stopping the fighting on all fronts. But the writer believes Trump and Netanyahu cannot be seen as 'losers' at home, and this is what weakens these efforts. His conclusion is that for now Netanyahu has the upper hand and the region is heading towards a new clash.
nazar: The oil that passes through Hormuz sets the price of everything in India from cooking gas to a farmer's diesel, and millions of Indian workers in the Gulf become less safe with every new threat. So this war is not distant news for us.

The article's most solid lesson is that wars often drag on more because of electoral arithmetic than because of the battlefield. The countries of South Asia, India included, should add their voice to these efforts for peace.
sawal: How many lives is one leader's election win worth?
ref: Strait of Hormuz
The narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil trade passes.
Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)
A powerful military force separate from Iran's regular army, answerable directly to the Supreme Leader.

h: If acid attacks are rising, the policy has failed: Supreme Court
dek: The Supreme Court told the Centre that issuing guidelines and leaving the job to the states is not enough, and that the open sale of acid must be rethought.
body: Hearing Shaheen Malik's petition on the rehabilitation of acid attack survivors on Tuesday, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana told the Union government plainly that if attacks are rising despite the guidelines, it means the policy has not served its purpose. The court asked for the whole policy to be reconsidered afresh in light of the National Crime Records Bureau's annual data.

For the Centre, Additional Solicitor General Archana Pathak Dave said detailed directions to stop retail sale had been sent to the states, but enforcement was a problem. The bench then asked why acid needs to be sold openly at all when many alternatives exist for household use. The court suggested three steps: first, find out what uses open sale was allowed for; then have experts look for alternatives; and where acid is essential, impose strict restrictions.

The hearing also took up an application from a woman lawyer at the Gauhati High Court, who alleges that a fellow lawyer threw acid on her in 2016. The sight in one of her eyes is badly affected, yet she continues to practise law. Appearing for her, Vrinda Grover said the amount under the victim compensation scheme is inadequate for any survivor.

On the allegation that Delhi's Sir Ganga Ram Hospital forcibly discharged a survivor, the court asked the hospital to look into arranging a room for her mother to stay in during the long treatment. The views of the Centre and NALSA were sought on a draft standard operating procedure proposed by an NGO.
nazar: Acid is still as easy to buy at a shop as it was ten years ago, and it is mostly women who pay the price. The court said what survivors have been saying for years: paper directions do not stop attacks, accountability does. Now we will see whether the Centre turns this into just another circular or actually reins in the sale.
sawal: Why is acid that no home really needs sold so openly?
ref: NALSA
The National Legal Services Authority, which runs free legal aid and compensation schemes for the poor and for victims.
NDPS Act
The 1985 law on narcotic substances, under which the sale of some drugs is tied to licences and records.

h: Umar Khalid's book removed from IISER Pune library
dek: A research book on Adivasi history was removed after a social media post; the institute called it a precaution.
body: The Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) in Pune has removed Umar Khalid's book Fractured Communities: Adivasi Histories and the Politics of Power from its library. Umar Khalid has been in jail without trial for more than six years in the alleged larger conspiracy case linked to the 2020 Delhi riots. The book came out this year and is based on his PhD thesis at JNU, which explores the history of Adivasi (indigenous) communities of Singhbhum under British rule.

The matter came up when an X account shared a photo of new arrivals at the library. On Sunday, Madabhushi Madan Gopal, chairman of the institute's Board of Governors, wrote that he was shocked the book had been included, that it had been withdrawn and that action had begun against those responsible. He also gave an assurance that this would not happen again.

On Monday the institute said in a statement that the step was taken as a precaution to avoid any misunderstanding or unrest. According to the institute, the library buys about 50 books every month on the recommendation of members and a committee.

Students at the institute have criticised the decision. They ask why a research book should be removed because of its author's name and not its content. According to the report, no fault in the book was pointed out; the decision was taken only on an online complaint.
nazar: A man has been kept in jail for six years without trial, and now even the history book he wrote cannot stay in a library. If books in a science institute start being removed on a troll's complaint, the question is not just about Umar Khalid. It is about the freedom without which a university is no longer a university.
sawal: Why fear a book before even reading it?
ref: IISER
Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, a chain of leading central government institutes for science education and research.

h: Notice to Centre on making all six verses of Vande Mataram compulsory
dek: A Buddhist activist and a former IAS officer say the Home Ministry's orders go against secularism and freedom of conscience.
body: The Supreme Court has issued notice to the Centre on petitions against two orders of the Union Home Ministry that make singing all six verses of Vande Mataram compulsory. Under these orders of 28 January and 9 July 2026, the full song is to be sung at formal government events, while for about 79 years the practice has been to sing only the first two verses.

The first petition is by B.D. Borkar, a Buddhist and civil rights activist from Nagpur. He argues that the first two verses were written before the novel Anandamath and only praise the beauty of the land, not any goddess or communal conflict. The other verses come from the novel, in which, according to the petition, the song turns into a prayer to a goddess and Muslims are portrayed as the enemy. Borkar has called the orders Islamophobic and harmful to fraternity.

The second petition is by Balakrishnan Sathyabhama Mavoji, a former IAS officer and president of an organisation working for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. He describes himself as from a Dalit Hindu community that does not follow sectarian traditions such as the Vaishnava and Shakta ones. He says forcing people to sing violates freedom of religion and conscience, and that the two-verse version is the one that became the national song by tradition.

A related petition by singer T.M. Krishna is also pending. It challenges an amendment that provides for up to three years in jail for obstructing the singing of Vande Mataram. The court has already said orally that no one who does not sing on grounds of conscience should be prosecuted. All the cases will be heard on 30 November.
nazar: Patriotism is built by giving equality, not by making people sing. Forcing the full version of a song on whose two verses there was agreement for decades, and holding out the fear of jail for not singing, tells a large section of people that their faith and conscience are second class in this country. It is good that Dalit and Buddhist voices are at the front of the challenge.
sawal: Can anyone's conscience be made to sing by order?
ref: Anandamath
Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's 1882 Bengali novel, which includes the song Vande Mataram.

h: Thousands of Adivasis march to Mantralaya for forests, water and schooling
dek: Led by the Shramjeevi Sanghatana, a Constitutional Rights Struggle March set off from Bhiwandi to Mumbai's Mantralaya.
body: Thousands of Adivasis (indigenous people) from Thane, Palghar, Raigad and Nashik districts began a march on foot on Tuesday afternoon from the Mumbai-Nashik highway towards Mantralaya, the state government headquarters in Mumbai. The Shramjeevi Sanghatana has named it the Constitutional Rights Struggle March. The organisation was founded by Vivek Pandit, and the march is led by its president Seeta Ghatale and working president Balaram Chaudhary. The first halt was set at Kharegaon.

People joined from areas such as Bhiwandi, Shahapur, Murbad, Vasai, Dahanu, Talasari, Vikramgad, Wada, Jawhar and Mokhada. About 250 police personnel were deployed, and heavy vehicles were barred from the highway.

Top of the demands is quick settlement of pending forest rights claims. They have also asked for free, good-quality, skill-building education for every Adivasi child up to the age of 18, a vidya sankul (education complex) in every taluka and drinking water in every Adivasi hamlet. The organisation says that despite huge spending on the Jal Jeevan Mission, women in many areas still carry water from far away.

According to Balaram Chaudhary, talks with the government brought positive assurances but no concrete decision. He said the movement will continue until a firm decision is taken on the pending demands. The report records no official response from the government.
nazar: Within a hundred kilometres of Mumbai's glitter there are villages where women walk miles for water and land titles stay stuck in files for years. That Adivasis must walk to the capital again and again with their most basic demands is the clearest exposure of the politics of assurances.
sawal: How many more years will forest rights claims stay pending?
ref: Forest Rights Act
A 2006 law that gives Adivasis and other traditional forest dwellers, who have lived in forests for generations, rights over land and forest.

h: News publishers move Supreme Court against data law
dek: Digital news publishers say the lack of a journalism exemption puts investigative reporting and confidential sources at risk; the court refused a stay.
body: The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) has challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and its 2025 rules in the Supreme Court. The association has 21 big digital publishers, including the Reliance group's Network18, the Adani group's NDTV, Indian Express, Times Internet, The Hindu and India Today.

The petition's main argument is that the law has no exemption for journalism. This could apply conditions such as giving notice, taking consent and deleting data even to journalists reporting in the public interest. Reporting on government officials, crime, business and governance could stop, and confidential sources risk being exposed. There is a special objection to Section 36, which gives the government broad power to demand information without court oversight and without telling the person affected. Concern has also been raised about the change to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act.
Senior advocate Madhavi Divan said the lack of an exemption amounts to a kind of prior censorship, while earlier drafts of the law had kept journalism out.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant refused to impose an interim stay without hearing the government, but issued notice on the stay application. The court said a balance must be struck between press freedom and privacy, and that media organisations may suggest safeguards against misuse. The next hearing is on 17 November.
nazar: Note the irony: the very houses whose channels long ago forgot how to question power are now crying out for press freedom. Still, the issue is real. A power like Section 36 will weigh heaviest on small independent journalists and RTI activists, who do not have big lawyers.
sawal: In the name of privacy, whose privacy is being protected?
ref: DPDP Act
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, which sets the rules for using people's personal data.
Section 8(1)(j)
A provision of the RTI Act that exempts personal information from disclosure; the DPDP Act has made it even broader.

h: Instagram blocks reel explaining Election Commission's affidavit
dek: LiveLaw's video was blocked in India citing a legal request, and restored after protest.
body: The legal news website LiveLaw said Instagram blocked one of its reels for viewers in India. The reel explained the Election Commission's position in the affidavit it filed in the Supreme Court on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The matter matters all the more because the SIR is being heard in the Supreme Court and the names of crores of voters are tied to it.
Instagram attached only a message saying it had received a legal request to restrict this content. It did not say which law the reel broke or who sent the request.

LiveLaw says the reel only explained the Commission's own position and did not even contain critical comment. The same video stayed available on YouTube. The outlet objected to the move on X, tagging Instagram and Meta.

It was later added to the story that Instagram had restored the video. In recent weeks there have been reports of several accounts and posts linked to the SIR protests being blocked on Instagram. For several hours before it was restored, viewers in India could not see the video, while it was open in the rest of the world. The platform gave no reason for the restoration either.
nazar: When a video explaining court proceedings, one that even carries the government's own side, is made to vanish without a reason, it shows that censorship no longer looks at what is said, only at the subject. Anonymous legal requests and silent platforms together are making news invisible, and no one has to answer for it.
sawal: Who sent that legal request, and why?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission's process of rebuilding the voter list, which faces allegations of names being deleted on a large scale.

h: Kochi crash: judge's son let off, four policemen suspended
dek: The 17-year-old accused in Kochi got bail at the police station itself; the government had to act after protests by the family and the public.
body: In Kochi a speeding Mercedes killed 55-year-old Jayabalakrishnan, who ran a small tea stall. The car was allegedly being driven by a 17-year-old boy whose father is an Additional District and Sessions Judge at the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal.

On the day of the crash the boy was given bail at the police station. The father was made the second accused only after strong protests. After the family and local people staged a sit-in at the police station, the police arrested the boy again, but the Juvenile Justice Board granted him bail once more. Relatives allege that the police took their phones, tried to delete videos and photos from after the detention, and mistreated them.

On Tuesday, Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala announced in the Assembly the suspension of four policemen of Cheranalloor police station: CI Shyamkumar, station house officer Vishwajith P.S., and constables Manoj K.P. and Arun Joy. He asked why a driver who killed a poor man was booked under sections that allow easy bail, and said the government would not defend police irresponsibility.

The action followed a preliminary report by ADGP (Law and Order) P. Vijayan, who visited the victim's family, the crash site and the police station to look into allegations of preferential treatment. The case has now been handed over to the District Crime Branch.
nazar: On one side an expensive car and a judge father, on the other a man who ran a tea stall. The speed with which the police first let the accused go shows that everyone being equal before the law is still only a promise. It should also be remembered that the suspensions came only when people took to the streets.
sawal: If people had not surrounded the police station, would the case have been buried right there?
ref: Juvenile Justice Board
The body that hears cases of accused persons under 18, working under the Juvenile Justice Act 2015.

h: Hateful comments on a girl's photo: RSS worker arrested in Kerala
dek: The comments were posted on Facebook under a photo of a young girl being honoured after she was selected for a national-level abacus competition.
body: Mulakkunnu police in Kerala have arrested Vimal Shivashakti, a resident of Azhiyur, who the report describes as an RSS worker. He is accused of posting sexually abusive and anti-Islam comments on Facebook targeting a young girl.

The comments were made under a photo showing the girl being honoured for being selected for a national-level abacus competition. In other words, a child's moment of success became a target for hate. What should have been a proud moment for the girl and her family was turned into public humiliation.
Young Democrats leader Yunus Vilakkode and the girl's father filed separate complaints. According to Vilakkode, a local court has sent the accused to judicial custody.

The report does not include a statement from the police, the sections of law applied, or the side of the accused or the RSS. The girl's age and the words of the comments are also not in the report. The details of the arrest and remand come from the complainant. The case is still at an early stage, and only further investigation will show what charges the accused faces.
nazar: Hate on social media now does not spare even children. In this case the arrest came quickly after the complaint, which is a relief, but most such comments float around without any action. Both platforms and police need to understand that online hate does real harm to real children.
sawal: Why should a little girl's success become a target of hate?
ref: Abacus
An old counting tool with beads, used to teach children fast mental maths. Competitions are held in it.

h: Adani's power plant in Pirpainti uproots Adivasi mango orchards
dek: In Bhagalpur's Pirpainti, Santhal and Sauria Paharia families who have lived for generations on land given for a coal power plant are losing their homes, livelihoods, water and ancestral sites.
body: In Pirpainti in Bihar's Bhagalpur district, about 479 hectares of land were given to Adani Power on a 33-year lease from August 2025, just a few months before the Assembly election. A 2,400 megawatt coal power plant is being built here, at an estimated cost of about Rs 28,225 crore. Construction has been under way since early 2026.

Villagers learnt of the project only when landowners began receiving money in December 2025. Of the 68 Adivasi (indigenous) families being displaced, 52 are Sauria Paharia, who are classed as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, and 16 are Santhal. These families have lived for generations on private land without leases. The company's environmental impact assessment mentions neither these Adivasis nor their resettlement.

The minutes of the January 2026 public hearing carry 447 signatures, but barely two of them are Sauria Paharia and not one is Santhal. A day before the hearing, Section 126 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita was applied against several vocal opponents. According to activist Shravan Singh, they were held until the hearing was over.

In the name of resettlement, 71 rooms of 10 by 12 feet have been built five kilometres away. Sunil Soren's family, who lived in five mud rooms, has been given one room, and Sanjhli Marandi asks where her goats and hens will go. People earned Rs 500 to 700 a day working in the orchards. Lakhs of mango trees were uprooted within a year.

Hand pumps are drying up, the water comes out yellow, and red dust from the digging settles everywhere. Sacred places such as the Jaher Than and the Devi Sthan, and the ancestral burial ground, are now inside the project area. At the end of September, seven Adivasis were arrested in an excise raid, which people see as pressure to move out. On 11 October the families were given leases for the new rooms and told to leave soon.
nazar: This story shows how the weakest people are left out of the count when big investments are announced. When an assessment does not even see the Adivasis, questions about the approval based on it are bound to arise. The Forest Rights Act and the consent of the gram sabha (village assembly) are not just rules on paper; they are a shield for exactly such moments.

One room in exchange for orchards, water, burial grounds and livelihoods is not justice. And while the country talks of moving away from coal, a new coal power plant is being built in Bihar at the cost of Adivasis.
sawal: How will orchards and ancestors fit into one room?
ref: Sauria Paharia
An Adivasi community living around the Rajmahal hills, recognised as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG). Their population in Bihar is very small.
Public hearing
The legal process of hearing the views of affected people before environmental clearance, conducted by the State Pollution Control Board.

h: Fish powder and stinking villages: coastal India's unheard fight
dek: Fishmeal factories that make feed for shrimp and salmon are bringing pollution, deaths and protests to coastal settlements from Goa to Tamil Nadu.
body: This part of a four-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project looks at India's fishmeal industry, which grinds small fish into feed for shrimp, salmon and chickens. There are more than 70 such factories in the country. Between 2018 and 2024, at least 30 factories were found linked to violations such as dumping dirty water into rivers and borewells, tax evasion and safety lapses, and there were at least 18 protests against them.

In Cuncolim, Goa, a company proposed a factory in August 2025 that would process at least 2,400 tonnes of fish every month. The municipal council and the local MLA opposed it, but the government, which had lifted a ban on new factories in 2024, bypassed the council in February 2026 and gave approval, with only a condition to install equipment to clean the gases.

In 2024, Pottalurani village in Tamil Nadu's Thoothukudi district protested for more than 175 days. People said the groundwater had been spoiled for four years. The election was boycotted, and a teacher who was leading the protest was transferred. Complaints of stench, polluted water and sick cattle were also recorded in Mukka in Karnataka and in Goa.

The main gas behind this stench is considered poisonous. By 2025, more than two and a half lakh people in the country lived within one and a half kilometres of these factories. Migrant workers have lost their lives inside the factories to suffocation, fires and explosions; for example, two workers were killed in a boiler blast in February 2022.

The sea is affected too. About a third of India's catch goes into feed. Pressure on oil sardine and mackerel has grown, though these same fish could have been cheap food for people in the country. Nearly all the shrimp goes abroad. The industry's association wants to triple production.
nazar: This is the same model of development in which the profit is exported, while the stench, illness and empty nets are left to the villages. When the objection of an elected local council is overturned from above, how can anyone trust environmental governance?
The fish on the plates of coastal fishing communities is going into feed for foreign shrimp farms. No talk of food security can dodge this question.
sawal: For whose plate is the village's fish being caught?
ref: Fishmeal
A powder made by drying and grinding small fish, used as feed in shrimp farming, fish farming and poultry farming.
The Outlaw Ocean Project
A US-based non-profit journalism organisation that investigates human rights and environmental abuses at sea.

h: Drought in the Thar: no sowing, and now the livestock are being sold
dek: After a weak monsoon in western Rajasthan, the fields lie empty, fodder costs twice as much and the dams are dry, but the government has still not declared a drought.
body: Chatar Singh Jam, a farmer in Jaisalmer, owns about a hundred bighas of land. In the kharif (monsoon) season it used to grow guar, moth, bajra and kachri, which brought in money and also fed the animals. This time the whole monsoon went by in waiting, and the sowing never happened. He says the soil does not even hold enough moisture for a rabi (winter) crop.

Western Rajasthan's khadin system, in which rainwater is held in the field to keep the soil moist, works only when there is some rain. This year it failed too. When the crop went, the fodder went with it: Chatar Singh says fodder has risen from six or seven rupees a kilo to fifteen or sixteen rupees. By his estimate, herders have already sold about twenty percent of their sheep and goats at half price, and by the next monsoon this share could reach sixty percent.

The weather department's figures show the same picture. Across the state, monsoon rain was 22 percent below normal, and in western Rajasthan 30 percent below. The shortfall was 59 percent in Jalore, 54 percent in Pali and 50 percent in Jaisalmer. In October, not a single drop fell in Barmer, Jalore, Nagaur and Pali.

Of the state's 693 dams, 216 are completely dry. On 8 October total storage was around 62 percent, against more than 90 percent at the same time last year. The 117 dams of the Jodhpur region hold only 16 percent water, compared with 80 percent a year ago.

Even so, the state government has not declared a drought. Panchayat (village council) elections are under way, and the opposition is demanding a declaration, pointing to Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. The report reminds us that animals sold out of distress will keep the herds from recovering for years to come.
nazar: The Thar economy rests on sheep, goats and camels, and when herders start selling their flocks at half price, this is not a crisis of one season but of many years. A drought declaration is not just a paper ritual. It is what opens up relief, fodder depots and extra work under MGNREGA.
Putting off this declaration in election season is an injustice to people who have neither the water nor the fodder to wait.
sawal: How many more animals must be sold before a drought is declared?
ref: Khadin
A traditional farming method of western Rajasthan, in which an earthen bund is built across a slope to hold rainwater in the field. A rabi crop is later sown in that stored moisture.
Drought declaration
A lack of rain alone is not enough; after assessing sowing, soil moisture and water, the state government declares a district or tehsil drought-hit, which starts the relief schemes.

h: In the Philippines, forests grow on paper while trees fall on the ground
dek: An investigation by Al Jazeera's 101 East and Lighthouse Reports finds that the Philippines' big greening programme missed most of its targets.
body: This is a 25-minute investigative film from 101 East, Al Jazeera's Asia-Pacific programme, released on 31 July 2026 on the Al Jazeera English YouTube channel. The reporter is Natasha Gutierrez. 101 East carried out the investigation together with Lighthouse Reports, an investigative journalism organisation, and Davao Today, a local publication from Mindanao in the Philippines.

The story begins in 2011. That year the Philippine government announced one of the world's most ambitious greening programmes, called the National Greening Program. The plan was to pay local people to plant crores of trees, have them look after the saplings, and raise forests again on barren land.

There is a long history behind this promise. In the twentieth century, unchecked logging and the spread of farming wiped out a large part of the Philippines' forests. The effects were plain to see in floods, landslides and farming in the hills. So the promise to bring the forests back was not only about the environment, but also about the livelihoods and safety of villages.

According to the film's description, the conclusion of this joint investigation, about fifteen years on, is that the programme failed to meet most of its targets. Satellite images of some of the areas that were meant to turn green tell the opposite story: there, forests appear to be cut rather than saved.

The second side of the investigation concerns the people who live on the land. The description says some Indigenous communities fear that the land their lives and livelihoods depend on could slip out of their hands. In other words, a government tree-planting drive could become a source of insecurity for the very people who have lived alongside the forest for generations.

Checking the data is central to this work. The data team of Lighthouse Reports and colleagues who examine supply chains are listed in the film's credits, which makes clear that the report rests not only on testimony but also on matching satellite images with documents.
The film points to a larger question: when tree-planting targets are measured in numbers, the real forest, its protection and the people who live in it are often left out of the count.
nazar: For India this film is a mirror. Here too, big figures for compensatory afforestation and tree planting are put forward, while old forests keep being cut for mines and projects. The count of saplings planted and the health of the forest that remains are not the same thing.

The biggest lesson is that forests do not survive without the communities that live in them. Any greening scheme that weakens the land rights of Adivasi (indigenous) people becomes a scheme not for the environment but for eviction.
sawal: When will governments that count trees start counting forests?
ref: National Greening Program
An afforestation programme of the Philippine government launched in 2011, which aimed to plant trees on a large scale on barren and degraded land by paying local people.
Lighthouse Reports
A non-profit investigative journalism organisation based in the Netherlands, which works with media houses around the world on joint investigations built on data and documents.

h: Tamanna's death: one house, one shrew and many silences
dek: The seventh part of Neha Naruka's series 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' probes the needless death of a young woman with satire and bitterness.
body: Neha Naruka's series 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' (Land of the Dead Souls) remembers, in each part, a woman whose life was taken by carelessness and indifference. The seventh part is about Tamanna, a hardworking and promising girl who got married, became pregnant within a year, and then died after an operation in a government hospital.

The story begins with a household quarrel. The creature the narrator was cursing as a rat is, according to the woman who works in the house, a shrew, and a pregnant one, so driving it out would be a sin. This shrew moves through the whole text like an unwanted landlady, and slowly becomes a bitter metaphor alongside Tamanna's story.

Everyone blames someone else for Tamanna's death. Her parents' family blames the stinginess of her in-laws, the in-laws blame the government doctors, and the doctors blame infection. In a beauty parlour, the narrator overhears two young mothers talking, one of whom says her husband will not even listen to talk of contraception. The face of a frightened girl of nineteen or twenty follows her all the way home.

Tamanna's mother weeps and says they were punished for some sin. The writer does not accept this logic: even if it was a punishment, why did it fall on an innocent daughter? Some deaths have no meaning to be found; they have to be swallowed, or else everyone's belly would become like Tamanna's.

At the end comes a metaphor: the roosters believed that morning came because of their crowing, but the sun rose anyway. And the hens who were not allowed to speak are now writing their own stories on paper, keyboards and phones.
nazar: This text takes a death out of the box marked 'fate' and puts the system in the dock: early marriage, a woman having no right over her own body, and the carelessness of the government hospital. Hindi needs writing like this, which gives anger the edge of satire and makes it readable.
sawal: Who will finally answer for Tamanna's death?
ref: Mritatmaon ka Desh
Neha Naruka's prose series (Land of the Dead Souls), each part about a woman who was lost to neglect and indifference.
Neha Naruka
Hindi poet; author of the poetry collection 'Phati Hatheliyan' (Cracked Palms) and winner of the 2024 Vagishwari Samman.

h: Silence hurts too: the walls inside a marriage
dek: The third part of Pallavi Vinod's 'Dampatya' series uses one couple's complaints to show how never learning to speak up hollows out a relationship.
body: Pallavi Vinod's column lets a husband and wife speak in turn. The husband says he treated his wife's family as his own, but she did not do the same for his. His younger sister's demands, his mother's old-fashioned thinking and the compulsion of living together are all part of his complaint.

The wife's story is different. Her sister-in-law takes fifteen to twenty thousand rupees every month, and when she asks about it, her husband shouts. She is taunted again and again about the savings spent on the wedding, when what she wanted more than jewellery and expensive saris was the freedom to live her own way. The man who was once her best friend now feels like a stranger.

The writer asks a counsellor friend whose fault it is. The answer is that it is not that simple. The real problem is that neither could say clearly what they meant, and both kept guessing at the other's meaning. Different homes have different rules, and sleep, food and ways of arguing all clash.

According to the counsellor, women today speak more openly, and a man who has never seen a woman speak up either fights more or goes silent. The writer sees this silence, called the 'silent treatment', as a deliberate wound, and tells the stories of two women in her family who were made to feel alone even in joint households.

Her argument is that the one who stays silent calls his restraint a virtue, but this too is a form of control. An unresolved hurt affects the other person's mind and body. In the end she asks: if a bird has to think before chirping in its own nest, what kind of home is that?
nazar: Inequality inside homes often runs not through raised voices but through silence. This piece gives that silence a name and reminds us that the question of equality reaches the kitchen and the sitting room too.
sawal: Is keeping quiet always the same as keeping the peace?
ref: Silent treatment
Punishing or ignoring someone by refusing to talk to them; psychology sees it as a form of emotional harm.

h: People of the third sky: five poems by Mayank Mishra
dek: Poems by a young poet from a village in Kushinagar touch on boredom, breaking, people on the margins and a mother's unseen labour.
body: Sammukh has published five poems by the young poet Mayank Mishra, his second appearance there. Mayank is from Pipra Mafi village in Kushinagar district, studied at Banaras Hindu University, and writes about the village, memory, loneliness and the lives of women.

'Oob ki Duniya' (The World of Boredom) is a poem about a day in which a man gets up, sits down, climbs stairs and looks at the clock, but nothing changes. The chair, the dust, the mirror and crumpled papers bear witness to that life going round in circles. 'Aakhir Mein Bach Jayega Main' (In the End, the Self Will Remain) speaks of the pile of lies, silences and buried desires left after death, where only questions remain about how we treated each other.

'Tootne ki Awaaz' (The Sound of Breaking) stands beside a building being torn down. Every brick has seen rain, laughter, insult and meals, and will now return to the soil. The poet feels this breaking inside himself too.

The sharpest poem in the set is 'Teesre Aakash ke Log' (People of the Third Sky). These are the people the market turns into a spectacle and sells, religion turns into examples, and politics turns into numbers. Even so, they laugh freely and swallow insults like dry bread.

The last poem, 'Maa ko Dekha' (I Saw Mother), uses images of the smallest space for the mother in the house's layout, the smoke of the kitchen and the starch water of rice to record the labour that no one counts.
nazar: In these poems, memories of the village come not as sentiment but as questions. The poet sees clearly the politics that turns people on the margins into numbers, and that is what makes these poems of our time.
sawal: When will the people turned into numbers be counted?
ref: Sammukh
A Hindi literary web magazine that publishes poetry, stories, criticism and translations.
