h: From the war of moustaches to Goebbels: seven poems by Anil Gangal
dek: Senior poet Anil Gangal's new poems question an age of arrogance, obedience, rumour and propaganda.
body: Anil Gangal's early poems appeared in magazines such as 'Lahar', 'Bindu' and 'Bhangima'. He has published six poetry collections, and 'Swad' (Taste) won the Rajasthan Sahitya Akademi's Sudhindra Award. Sammukh has published seven of his new poems together.

In 'Moonchhon ke Yuddh' (The War of Moustaches), the moustache is a sign of arrogance and unspoken command that drives decisions at home, in the office, in the Assembly and even in the police station. The same swagger shows up in fights over religion, language, caste and knowledge, and ends only at the cremation ground. 'Farmabardari' (Obedience) shows how asking 'why' is slowly removed from speech and given the name of good manners.

'Aadim Yug ki Santanen' (Children of the Primitive Age) says that despite smartphones and the Constitution, herd thinking and the habit of pushing the weak aside survive in us, and a single rumour can wipe out centuries of learning in a day. In 'Goebbels', propaganda no longer needs uniforms or loudspeakers; lies come through the phone, and there is no need to burn books when no one opens them anyway.

In 'Mritakon ki Aankhen' (The Eyes of the Dead), the dead do not ask for revenge; they only watch who kept their integrity and who sold it. 'Patjhad Mein Bacha Aakhiri Patta' (The Last Leaf Left in Autumn) and 'Kunba' (The Clan) give the set a personal and family colour, where the family is a living document that each generation rewrites with its questions.
nazar: These poems speak directly to our times: when asking questions is called rudeness and lies are made into truth by repetition, the job of poetry is to keep the conscience awake. Gangal does this without sloganeering.
sawal: When and how did 'why' disappear from our speech?
ref: Goebbels
The propaganda minister of Nazi Germany, whose name is linked to the policy of turning lies into truth by repeating them again and again.

h: Lost films: the forgotten links between Hindi fiction and cinema
dek: Dinesh Shrinet remembers films of the seventies that were made from Hindi literature and then almost forgotten.
body: The early seventies were a special time in the relationship between Hindi literature and cinema. Directors from the Pune film institute were experimenting, and the 'Nayi Kahani' (New Story) movement had prepared the ground for complex, lonely middle-class characters. Everyone remembers films like 'Uski Roti', 'Sara Akash' and 'Rajnigandha', but Dinesh Shrinet sets out to look for films of which not even a proper record survives.

Mrinal Sen made 'Oka Oori Katha' from Premchand's 'Kafan' (The Shroud), and it can still be watched today. But Ramesh Gupta's 1978 film of Jainendra Kumar's novel 'Tyagpatra' (The Resignation) is now missing. The writer remembers its advertisements on the radio from his childhood. Vidya Sinha played Mrinal, a woman who rejects the old morality.

Kamleshwar's 'Badnam Basti' (1971) was found again after nearly fifty years in the dark, and drew new interest in the context of queer movements around the world. No print of Girish Ranjan's 'Dak Bangla' (1974) has been found yet. The writer reads the dak bungalow (a government rest house) as a metaphor: a place to stop, not a home, like the relationships of that woman, which have no stability.
He sees Shivendra Sinha's 'Phir Bhi' (1971) as an early attempt at parallel cinema, with experiments in freeze frames, negatives and montage. No print of it can be found either.

The writer concludes that prints, reviews and records are so scarce that it is hard to give a final verdict on these films, but without finding them, the history of the relationship between Hindi literature and cinema will remain incomplete.
nazar: This piece reminds us that cultural memory does not survive on its own. Films that did not reach the market or festivals were wiped out, and with them the screen versions of many bold Hindi stories. The real demand of pieces like this is public investment in film archives.
sawal: Who will search for our lost films?
ref: Nayi Kahani
A Hindi fiction movement of the 1950s and 60s; Mohan Rakesh, Kamleshwar and Rajendra Yadav were its leading names.
FTII
The Film and Television Institute of India in Pune, which produced many directors of parallel cinema.

h: Back in the village: why ask a girl about the kitchen first?
dek: Nikita Yadav's memoir records the patriarchy, poverty and damage from alcohol she saw on returning to her village after her studies.
body: After finishing her studies at the University of Hyderabad, Nikita Yadav returns to her village after a year and a half. The roads, fields and houses are the same; what has changed is how she sees them. Everyday customs now look to her like questions of society, patriarchy and inequality.

She visits the home of a childhood classmate. Her friend's mother greets her with great affection, but most of her questions are about cooking, farming and running a home, not about her studies or dreams. The writer wonders why these questions are asked only of girls; no one asks boys whether they will manage the home along with a job.

That mother climbs the stairs despite pain in her legs and cooks every day for several men. The writer is saddened that this labour has been taken as her duty alone. On the way back, her friend tells her that he had to drop out of studies because his family did not support him; his brother earns but blows the money on fun, and his father is drowning in drink.

The writer remembers her school days, when many classmates said their families could not afford further studies. Now she sees that the problem is not of one household but of the whole system: education getting costlier, poverty, and alcohol spreading among young people and even children in the village, followed by violence at home.

The deepest wound is that it is older women themselves who teach new brides to keep enduring. In the writer's view, this is patriarchy's biggest success. Her anger is not at that mother but at the system that asks girls about the kitchen and boys about their dreams.
nazar: This memoir shows how the eyes of a girl who has reached higher education read the village afresh. Her testimony on alcohol, costly education and domestic violence questions policies that see village women only as figures in government schemes.
sawal: When will boys be asked about housework?
ref: Bela
Hindwi's prose section, which publishes memoirs, essays, travel writing and criticism.
